beats.intro: Lesson six. [[sub]]How to find the activities that multiply your team's output, and how to delegate without letting go of the result.
beats.lever: Every activity takes some of your time. [[hours]]Here are five hours of a manager's week. [[out]]Each one adds something to the team's output, but not the same amount. [[lev]]The multiplier is leverage: how much output an activity creates. [[sum]]Your output is the sum: each activity times its leverage, added up.
beats.three: So there are three ways to get more output from your hours. [[fast]]Do things faster. That is the next lesson. [[raise]]Raise the leverage of what you already do. [[mix]]Or shift your time from low-leverage activities to high ones.
beats.many: Where does high leverage come from? [[one]]First, when one manager affects many people. [[plan]]A finance manager designs the annual planning process: what each group must bring, and who does what. [[fan]]That work shapes the work of some two hundred people. [[talk]]Teaching works the same way. Grove spends two hours telling two hundred new employees how the company works. A sales trainer who does the job badly does damage just as widely.
beats.timing: Leverage depends on timing. [[early]]Done before planning starts, the finance manager's work clears up confusion for everyone. [[late]]Done later, scrambling to help one manager at a time, it is worth far less. [[quit]]The same is true when a valued person says they are quitting. Act at once, or the chance is gone.
beats.brief: Second, a short action can shape someone's work for a long time. [[rev]]A performance review takes a few hours to prepare and deliver. [[long]]It can steer a person's work for a year. [[neg]]Done badly, it can discourage them for just as long. [[tick]]Even a simple reminder file, set up once, keeps paying off indefinitely.
beats.unique: Third, unique knowledge. [[price]]Grove's example is the engineer who sets prices. [[high]]Set them too high, and hundreds of salespeople cannot win business. [[low]]Too low, and the company gives money away. [[stat]]Or think of the one statistician whose sample-size calculation sets the size of every clinical study. [[spec]]Like Grove's process engineer, geologist or actuary, specialists like these have enormous leverage over the work of others.
beats.q2: Quick check. Name the source of leverage.
beats.negative: Leverage can also be negative. [[prep]]Arrive unprepared at a meeting you lead, and you waste everyone's time, and what they could have done with it. [[mood]]A manager who sinks into gloom spreads it through the whole group, often without noticing. [[waffle]]And a manager who waffles on a decision stops everyone waiting on it. [[light]]No green light is a red light. [[hard]]Bad training can be fixed with retraining. Gloom and waffling are much harder to undo.
beats.meddle: Meddling is negative leverage too. [[see]]Suppose you spot a bad trend in your report's area, [[dict]]and you dictate exactly what to do. [[again]]Do it often, [[shrink]]and your report starts to see their job more narrowly, [[up]]bringing problems to you instead of solving them. [[less]]In the long run, the group produces less.
beats.art: So the art of management is choosing. [[many]]Among many activities that look equally important, [[pick]]pick the one, two or three with leverage far beyond the rest, and put your effort there. [[comp]]For Grove, that meant customer complaints. Each needs follow-up from someone. [[dig]]But which one in ten or twenty to dig into himself was a matter of judgment: a sense that behind this one lie deeper problems.
beats.delegate: Delegation is leverage, too. [[base]]But it only works when you and the person taking the task share the same information, [[ideas]]and the same sense of how to solve problems. [[gap]]Without that, they can only follow detailed instructions, [[low]]and that has low leverage, just like meddling.
beats.pencil: Picture handing someone a pencil, [[hold]]and not letting go. [[enjoy]]We all hold on to some tasks because we enjoy them. That is fine, if you decide it consciously. [[fake]]What hurts is pretending to delegate while still holding on. [[know]]Which tasks should you hand over? [[best]]Grove's answer: the ones you know best, because those are the easiest for you to monitor. It will feel wrong. Do it anyway.
beats.abdicate: Because delegating without follow-through is abdication. [[still]]Once you hand over a task, you are still responsible for the result. [[mon]]Monitoring is how you make sure, and monitoring is not meddling. Grove's staff reviews of delegated programs were exactly this. [[draft]]Monitor at the lowest-value stage, just as on a production line. [[rough]]Read the rough draft, not the polished report, so a basic problem costs little to fix.
beats.sample: How often should you check? [[new]]Often when the task is new to that person, [[exp]]less as their work on it proves itself. Base it on their experience with this task, not their ability in general. Grove calls this task-relevant maturity, a later lesson. [[rand]]And check details at random. Checking everything is like testing every unit that leaves the factory. [[cap]]To delegate a decision, monitor the thinking behind it: ask specific questions about a spending request, and approve it when the answers hold up.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Output is each activity times its leverage, added up. [[w2]]Leverage comes from reaching many people, a brief act with a long effect, or unique knowledge. [[w3]]Timing matters, and leverage can be negative: waffling, gloom, meddling. [[w4]]Delegate what you know best, and keep monitoring. [[w5]]Check rough drafts, at random, more often for new tasks. Now the lesson practice.
